strengths: Addresses an important and timely question about when Gaussian universality breaks down in high-dimensional ERM, with clear practical relevance
Novel and insightful characterization: the decomposition x^T θ̂ ≈ x^T μ* + α*z precisely identifies when score Gaussianity holds (iff x^T μ* is Gaussian)
Clear distinction among three types of universality (performance, score, minimizer) with comprehensive related work survey in Table 1
Compelling empirical examples (Figures 1-2) demonstrating failures of universality on both synthetic (bimodal) and real (MNIST) data
Heuristic extension of CGMT to non-Gaussian settings via clever decomposition θ̂ = μ_θ̂ + θ_0, creating a general framework for non-Gaussian analysis
Rigorously proven subsidiary results (Theorems 2.1, 3.3, 7.1) and supporting lemmas with comprehensive appendix proofs
Extends beyond squared ℓ2 loss to general convex losses and smooth convex regularizers, improving scope relative to prior work
weaknesses: Critical Issue: Claim 4.1 (central to main results) is stated as 'still only a conjecture' rather than rigorously proven, undermining the soundness of Theorems 4.3, 4.4, and 6.1 which depend on it

Critical Issue: Assumption 4 (minimizer universality) is assumed without proof, with the authors noting 'a proof of this result based on Chatterjee's normal-approximation method is under preparation', creating a gap in the logical chain for score universality characterization
Limited practical impact: Section 5 shows performance universality still holds for squared ℓ2 loss (most common case) even when score universality fails, reducing consequences of the breakdown

Restrictive scope: Assumption 2 excludes non-smooth penalties (e.g., Lasso), Assumption 3 requires bounded third derivatives, and Assumption 1 requires Gaussian concentration properties—limiting real-world applicability
Assumption 4 introduced late (Section 6) despite being essential for main results; status of Claim 4.1 as conjecture not sufficiently highlighted in main text

Missing practical details: no algorithms for solving the min-max problem (Eq. 6), handling numerical issues in Q(ν) computation, or guidance for practitioners implementing Theorem 4.4's fixed-point system
Experiments mostly illustrative; limited comprehensive validation across different loss functions, regularizers, and data distributions compared to scope of theoretical claims

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant question about when Gaussian universality holds in high-dimensional ERM
Provides clear characterization (Theorem 6.1): score universality holds iff x^⊤μ* is Gaussian, offering sharp understanding of universality breakdown
Distinguishes three types of universality clearly and develops comprehensive theoretical framework
Theorem 3.3 (quadratic universality of regularizers) is solid and cleanly extends to non-Gaussian settings
Ambitious technical contribution attempting to extend CGMT to non-Gaussian designs
Provides empirical validation on synthetic and real data (MNIST) demonstrating non-universality phenomena
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Theorem 6.1 (main result) depends entirely on Assumption 4 (minimizer universality), which is unproven. Authors explicitly state proof is 'under preparation'—this violates standards of mathematical rigor expected at top venues
CRITICAL: Claim 4.1 (generalized CGMT), which is foundational for Theorem 4.3, is stated as 'still only a conjecture' in Appendix C. Main theorems cannot rest on unproven conjectures
Assumption 4 justified only heuristically via equation (8), lacking rigorous derivation despite being essential to main results
Condition 3 of Claim 4.1 (stability bound with τ independent of p,n) is stated without verification of when/why it holds
Limited experimental validation: only synthetic bimodal data and binary MNIST classification; no systematic scaling studies or evidence that Assumption 4 holds
Restrictive assumptions: Assumption 2 excludes Lasso and non-smooth regularizers; Assumption 1 requires Lipschitz transforms of Gaussians (excludes heavy-tailed data); C³ regularizers required
Proof of uniqueness for fixed-point system (Theorem 4.4) not provided; claimed without justification
Critical limitations buried: Assumption 4's unproven status not highlighted in main text; Claim 4.1 being conjecture only mentioned in appendix
Practical limitations: computing the fixed-point system (Theorem 4.4) is implicit and not obviously easier than solving original ERM; no algorithms or computational complexity provided
Incomplete finite-n analysis: results are purely asymptotic; Theorem 2.1 provides concentration but main results lack convergence rates

Limited comparison to recent related work (Dandi et al. 2023, Mallory et al. 2025); advantage over AMP-based methods not clearly articulated

strengths: Addresses important gap: provides explicit characterization of when Gaussian universality breaks down in high-dimensional ERM, a practically important question
Unified framework elegantly extends CGMT to non-Gaussian settings via concentration (Assumption 1); systematic treatment of three universality notions is exemplary
Key conceptual insight: Theorem 6.1 characterization that test score is Gaussian iff x^T μ* is Gaussian; elegant and immediately useful
Comprehensive technical development: quadratic regularizer approximation (Theorem 3.3) is clean; decomposition θ̂ = μ_θ̂ + θ₀ is clever; fixed-point characterization generalizes prior RMT results
Convincing empirical validation: bimodal and MNIST experiments demonstrate theory works and that Gaussian universality fails in practice; theoretical predictions track empirical observations well
Exceptional presentation of related work: Table 1 provides systematic comparison across dimensions and methods; clarifies relationship between RMT, AMP, and CGMT perspectives
Generality of framework: covers regression/classification, general convex losses, various regularizers, correlated non-Gaussian features
Geometric results (Theorem 7.1) provide interpretable sufficient conditions for score universality via subspace confinement
weaknesses: Claim 4.1 (generalized CGMT for concentrated designs) is presented as unproven conjecture, yet it is foundational for Theorem 4.3 (main result); convex analysis derivation in Appendix C lacks rigor of complete proof; should either prove rigorously, establish partial results, or more transparently discuss why conjecture is believed (noting this is standard in CGMT literature)

Assumption 4 (minimizer universality) is itself a universality assumption—the very phenomenon being studied—creating circularity; justified only by 'no empirical counterexamples' which is weak; proof via Chatterjee's method is 'under preparation' but should appear in paper or be substantially sketched

Limited practical guidance: while Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 7.2 give conditions for when universality holds, limited intuition on when breakdown occurs; few design principles for constructing data/models manifesting breakdown

Regularity conditions restrictive: Assumption 2 excludes important cases like Lasso; Assumption 3 bounds third derivatives with C^{-1/2} factors in off-diagonal components; no discussion of extension to these cases

Fixed-point equations (Theorem 4.4) require solving saddle-point system with high-dimensional expectations; no guidance on numerical solution strategies or practical computation; unclear how practitioners would use results
Finite-sample analysis minimal: concentration bounds (Theorem 2.1) are main result; convergence rates not quantified (only limits shown); unclear when asymptotics 'kick in' for practical n,p values

Experimental scope limited: synthetic experiments relatively simple (bimodal mixture); only MNIST as real data; no computational complexity analysis or timing comparisons; no comparison with other non-Gaussian approaches

Presentation improvements possible: deterministic equivalent J (Eq. 4) is complex; more intuitive motivation before formal statement would help; Moreau envelope notation may need more explanation; relationship between min-max form (Eq. 6) and fixed-point system could be more direct

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: characterizing when Gaussian universality holds in high-dimensional ERM, with direct practical implications
Provides a comprehensive unifying framework connecting RMT, CGMT, and AMP approaches, clarifying their relationships
Clear theoretical characterization: Theorem 6.1 elegantly shows x^T θ̂ is Gaussian iff x^T μ* is Gaussian, with useful distinction between performance/score/minimizer universality
Good empirical validation within scope: Figures 1-2 convincingly demonstrate universality breakdown on elastic loss and MNIST
Rigorous technical execution of concentration arguments using Poincaré inequalities with detailed proofs in appendix
Useful special cases: Section 5 shows performance universality can hold when score universality fails, providing important intuition
weaknesses: Main theoretical results (Theorems 4.3, 6.1) are conditional on Claim 4.1, which is explicitly stated as an unproven conjecture about generalized CGMT for non-Gaussian designs. Three verification conditions are asserted but not proved.

Theorem 6.1's full characterization of test scores relies on Assumption 4 (minimizer universality), which is assumed rather than rigorously proved. Authors acknowledge proof is 'under preparation' (Louart 2026), leaving a critical gap.

Restrictive assumptions exclude important practical cases: Assumption 2 requires smoothness/strict convexity (excluding Lasso and sparse methods); Assumption 3 excludes some structured regularizers. These limitations undermine practical applicability.

Limited technical novelty: CGMT extension is heuristic rather than rigorous; proof techniques largely standard (concentration inequalities, fixed-point analysis). Main contribution is framework rather than new tools.

Experimental validation is thin: mostly synthetic examples (bimodal data, elastic loss); only one real dataset (MNIST) with minimal details. No computational analysis of fixed-point equations or large-scale validation.

Missing practical guidance on when universality breaks down: Theorem 6.1 characterizes the condition but provides limited intuition. Theorem 7.1 only addresses signal-plus-noise models with limited scope.

Presentation is dense and difficult to follow: distinction between rigorously proved and conditional results could be much clearer upfront. Jumping between min-max (Theorem 4.3) and fixed-point formulations (Theorem 4.4) without sufficient explanation.
Fixed-point equations in Theorem 4.4 lack computational details: how to solve? What are existence/uniqueness conditions? No algorithmic guidance provided.
Reproducibility issues: code availability mentioned but no link; MNIST experimental details minimal; verification of Assumption 1 for specific data models requires additional work.

strengths: Addresses important problem of characterizing Gaussian universality breakdown in high-dimensional ERM
Clear conceptual framework distinguishing three types of universality with comprehensive literature comparison (Table 1)
Interesting theoretical insight that performance universality can hold without score universality (Corollary 5.1)
Novel covariance-adjusted subspace confinement result (Theorem 7.1)
Well-articulated connections among RMT, AMP, and CGMT perspectives
Extensive technical development with detailed proofs in appendices
weaknesses: Critical flaw: All main results (Theorems 4.3, 4.4, 6.1) are conditional on Claim 4.1, which is explicitly stated as an unproven conjecture—not a theorem. This undermines the validity of the main theoretical contributions

Circular reasoning: Assumption 4 (minimizer universality) is used to prove Theorem 6.1 (score universality), yet Assumption 4 itself is unproven and justified only by stating 'no empirical counterexamples known' with proof 'under preparation'
Limited experimental validation: Only synthetic examples (p=30, n=50) and MNIST binary classification. Missing experiments on larger dimensions, multiple datasets, and multiple random seeds

Lack of practical guidance: Results characterize asymptotics through implicit fixed-point equations with no discussion of how practitioners would use these results or verify when universality breaks down

Technical rigor issues: Several derivations are formal rather than rigorous; max-min interchanges and taking derivatives lack full justification; uniqueness/stability of saddle points assumed but not proven

Unclear practical relevance: Restriction to convex problems and concentrated data excludes important settings (heavy-tailed, non-convex). No computational complexity analysis for solving fixed-point equations

Presentation weakness: Conjectural nature of main results not sufficiently emphasized. Readers may not realize all main theorems depend on Claim 4.1. Assumptions presented without adequate justification in main text
Scope limitations: Requires smooth strongly convex regularizers (excluding Lasso), concentrated data (excluding heavy-tailed), and convex problems (excluding modern deep learning)

strengths: Novel framework explicitly characterizing when Gaussian universality breaks down in high-dimensional ERM through the elegant criterion: x⊤θ̂ is Gaussian if and only if the projection x⊤μ* is Gaussian
Rigorous mathematical development with careful distinction between three types of universality (performance, score, minimizer), providing valuable conceptual clarity to the landscape
Broad applicability across general convex losses, correlated non-Gaussian data with concentration properties, and smooth strongly convex regularizers—exceeding prior work in scope

Comprehensive and honest treatment of assumptions: conditional results are clearly delineated, unproven claims (Claim 4.1 on non-Gaussian CGMT, Assumption 4 on minimizer universality) are explicitly acknowledged as conjectures/assumptions
Successfully recovers fixed-point equations from RMT, AMP, and prior CGMT work, validating the framework and demonstrating its unifying power
Exceptional presentation with clear motivation (compelling examples in Figures 1-2), excellent organization (Table 1 survey), and comprehensive appendices containing full proofs

Actionable insights including: (i) performance universality can hold despite score non-Gaussianity (ridge regression), (ii) covariance-adjusted confinement reveals non-trivial geometric effects, (iii) identification of sources of non-Gaussianity in test scores
Real-data validation on MNIST demonstrating that moment-matching fails in practice, enhancing practical relevance beyond toy examples
weaknesses: Core results (Theorems 4.3, 4.4) critically depend on unproven Claim 4.1 (generalized CGMT for non-Gaussian designs), presented as conjecture. While natural and transparent, this is a foundational limitation affecting reproducibility and certainty of main claims

Theorem 6.1's characterization of universality breakdown requires unproven Assumption 4 (minimizer universality). Authors note proof is 'under preparation' but not available for review—this is a significant gap that substantially strengthens the paper if resolved

Performance universality results are limited in scope: only rigorously established for squared loss (Section 5); for general losses requires assuming score universality or asymptotic Gaussianity, substantially narrowing practical applicability

Inapplicable to non-smooth penalties (excludes Lasso and related methods) and requires smooth regularizers with bounded third derivatives (Assumption 3), limiting scope compared to modern machine learning

Limited empirical validation: only two experiments (synthetic bimodal data, MNIST) with no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported. Additional real datasets and losses would strengthen claims

Presentation is technically dense with heavy notation (Moreau envelopes, proximal operators, tensor spectral norms) that limits accessibility to practitioners. Intuition for why the non-Gaussian CGMT extension should hold is underdeveloped

Incomplete reproducibility: promised code not yet available; experimental details sparse (number of trials, computational cost, parameter sensitivity analysis missing); theoretical reproducibility depends on unproven assumptions
The practical scope of results is constrained to the proportional regime (p = Θ(n)) with convex losses only—neural networks and other non-convex settings excluded
